newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: Mandela's gesture to Buthelezi seen boosting peace.
newsitem.headline: Mandela's gesture to Buthelezi seen boosting peace.

text.p: Nelson Mandela's appointment of rival Mangosuthu Buthelezi to stand in as South African president will boost peace between their bitter supporters, analysts said.

Buthelezi, leader of the mainly Zulu Inkatha Freedom Party, said he was "filled with awe" by Mandela's Friday announcement that he should run the country when the president and his deputy attend the World Economic Forum in Switzerland next week.
Under the constitution, if his deputy is also unavailable, Mandela can appoint any cabinet minister to stand in for him.
Analysts said the appointment was a public show of his faith in Buthelezi, which would boost the flagging peace process in KwaZulu-Natal where their supporters have battled for years.
Inkatha is a junior partner in the coalition government led by Mandela's African National Congress (ANC) and Buthelezi is interior minister.
But that has not stopped him from being one of the ruling party's fiercest critics.

"This will increase the cooperation between the ANC and Inkatha and perhaps normalise their relationship now that Mandela has shown he has confidence in Buthelezi as a leader," said Thabo Sabela, politics professor at the University of Zululand.
Buthelezi said in a statement he hoped not to betray that confidence.
"I also pray to the Lord that nothing happens in the few hours during which I will be holding such a responsibility to show that I did not deserve that trust," he said.
University of Natal political analyst Alexander Johnston said Mandela's choice was a shrewd move.

"When Mandela looks for ways to be conciliatory he often makes things difficult for his enemies," he said. "Mandela has now put the onus on Buthelezi to find an appropriate response, a positive response."
Buthelezi's party has been rocked by internal divisions, but he has denied his autocratic style of leadership was pushing the party into crisis.

A number of senior members quit in recent weeks and analysts are predicting more defections. South African newspapers reported on Friday that Buthelezi was insisting members sign an oath of allegiance ahead of an important party meeting next week.
But party members said there was no such thing.

"There is no loyalty pledge. It is a straightforward letter to members of parliament, provincial MPs and senators asking if they will be eligible for the 1999 elections if they were chosen by the party," said parliamentarian Velaphi Ndlovu.
Johnston said Buthelezi's appointment as acting president, albeit for a brief period, should give his standing a boost.
"Inkatha's problems will not be resolved completely by something like this. They face very difficult times but this will help in the short term."
